sections.h2: Where is Starkville, Mississippi, and what drives its housing?
sections.html:
Starkville is the county seat of Oktibbeha County in east-central Mississippi, and it is closely tied to Mississippi State University. The university, founded in 1878 as the state's land-grant school, turned a farming town into a college town, and that shapes who buys, rents and sells houses here.

The city had 24,360 residents at the 2020 census and is the largest city in the Golden Triangle region. Its median age was 28.7, and 40.8 percent of households were people living alone. Oktibbeha County as a whole had 51,427 people.

Wikipedia describes the economy as centered on advanced research, manufacturing, retail and tourism that the university population supports. For a seller, that means the buyer pool, the rental pool and the calendar of the academic year all matter.

sections.h2: How does the college calendar affect a Starkville home sale?
sections.html:
A house near campus tends to be shown to students, parents, faculty and investors, while a house farther out is shown mostly to families and staff. The 2020 census counted 13,670 housing units in Starkville, and 17.5 percent of them were vacant. The rental vacancy rate was 15.9 percent and the homeowner vacancy rate was 2.7 percent.

Those two numbers differ sharply: homes held by owners were vacant far less often than rentals. A landlord with a house that has been sitting vacant between leases is often the seller most pressed for time.

  • Leases that end in May or August can create an easy handoff, or a vacant house that carries bills.
  • If tenants are in place at closing, the lease terms matter to the buyer, so gather the lease and rent records early.
  • A house that needs work between tenants may sell more cleanly to an as-is buyer than to a retail buyer with a lender.

Starkville's Cotton District, begun in 1969 as a New Urbanist neighborhood, is a compact, walkable area with thousands of residential units near downtown, and it contains many restaurants and bars.

sections.h2: Which roads, schools and services come with a Starkville address?
sections.html:
U.S. Route 82 runs east to west across the north side of the city as a bypass, and Mississippi Highways 12 and 25 also pass through. U.S. 82 leads about 25 miles east to Columbus. Golden Triangle Regional Airport has the nearest scheduled service, and George M. Bryan Field handles general aviation.

Public schools belong to the Starkville Oktibbeha Consolidated School District, formed in 2015 when the former Starkville and Oktibbeha County districts merged. Its schools in the city include Sudduth Elementary, Henderson Ward Stewart Elementary, Overstreet Elementary, Partnership Middle School, Armstrong Junior High and Starkville High School. Private options include Starkville Academy and Starkville Christian School.

The city is run by a mayor and seven aldermen elected to four-year terms. Twenty-two sites in Starkville are listed on the National Register of Historic Places, so it is worth asking early whether an older house near downtown has any historic designation attached.

sections.h2: How does property tax work for a Starkville house?
sections.html:
Oktibbeha County values and collects the tax, and the bill is due by February 1 for the previous assessment year. The County Tax Assessor and Collector share an office at 101 East Main Street in Starkville, reachable at 662-323-1273.

The Mississippi Constitution sets the assessment ratios. A single-family, owner-occupied home is Class I at 10 percent of true value. Other real property, such as a house rented to students, is Class II at 15 percent. Multiply the assessed value by the combined millage of the county, city and school district to get the bill.

That ratio gap is a practical concern for landlords here. A rental house is taxed on a larger share of its value than a house its owner lives in, and a house that stops being owner-occupied can lose its homestead credit. Assessors must revalue real property at least every four years, and a value dispute goes to the county Board of Supervisors, normally by the first Monday in August before the tax is due.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about homestead exemption and taxes at closing?
sections.html:
Homestead exemption is tied to the owner who lives in the house on January 1, so it does not pass to the next owner. Each new owner has to apply at the Tax Assessor's office between January 1 and April 1.

The state's eligibility rules include owning and occupying the house as a primary residence on January 1, with the deed filed with the Chancery Clerk before January 7. The regular tier gives a credit of up to $300 for owners under 65. Owners 65 or older or totally disabled are exempt on the first $7,500 of assessed value, and some veterans and surviving spouses receive a full exemption.

For an investor buying a Starkville rental, none of this applies, because the house will not be a primary residence. For a family buying their first home, a closing in the first months of the year can mean waiting until the next year for the credit.

Unpaid taxes can lead to a tax sale. State rules allow sales on the first Monday in April and the last Monday in August, and the county Tax Collector handles the details.

sections.h2: What does Mississippi require a Starkville seller to disclose, and what are the sale options?
sections.html:
Under Section 89-1-503 of the Mississippi Code, the seller gives the buyer a written property condition disclosure statement as soon as practicable before title transfers. If the buyer receives it after making an offer, the buyer has three days after hand delivery, or five days after mailing, to withdraw the offer in writing.

A Starkville owner generally has three paths. The first is a retail listing, which can work well near campus when the house is in good order and the calendar is right. The second is selling to another investor, which suits a rental with tenants. The third is a direct as-is sale to a cash buyer, which skips repairs, showings and lender conditions.

Starkville's history is also tied to the university. The area was chosen for the agricultural college because of its farming, timber, cattle and dairy output, and the city later became a college town. If a house has been in a family for years, old deeds, unrecorded transfers and shared heirs are worth checking during the title search.

Whatever you choose, order a title search. An attorney or title company can find unpaid taxes, mortgages and liens, and prepare the deed. The Chancery Clerk records the deed, and it needs a notarized seller signature and a legal description.

Cash Home Buyers talks with Starkville sellers about as-is sales, including houses with tenants or deferred repairs. We lay out what we can do and when, so you can compare it with listing.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Starkville rental house with tenants in it?
faqs.a: Yes. The buyer takes the house subject to the existing lease, so you need to hand over the lease, deposit information and rent records. Some buyers prefer a vacant house, so talk through timing before you commit.

faqs.q: When are Oktibbeha County property taxes due?
faqs.a: They are due on or before February 1 for property assessed in the preceding year. If February 1 falls on a weekend or holiday, payment the next Monday carries no penalty.

faqs.q: Is a Starkville rental taxed differently from a home I live in?
faqs.a: Yes. Under the Mississippi Constitution an owner-occupied single-family home is assessed at 10 percent of true value, while other real property is assessed at 15 percent.

faqs.q: Do I have to disclose problems when I sell in Mississippi?
faqs.a: Most sellers must deliver a written property condition disclosure statement before title transfers. A buyer who gets it late can cancel the offer within three days of hand delivery or five days of mailing.
